questions.q:
A district atlas team records four sites before drawing its landform page.
Site P: 120 m above sea level; wide, flat farmland with no large hills or deep valleys.
Site Q: 900 m above sea level; a broad top that is more or less flat, with a steep slope on its eastern side.
Site R: 650 m above sea level; gentle slopes and a rounded top, much lower than the snowy peaks to its north.
Site S: 3,800 m above sea level; a broad base, steep slopes and a narrow summit, snow-covered in winter.
(a) Which landform should the team print for Site P and for Site Q?
(b) One member wants to label Site R 'mountain' because it rises above the fields around it. Correct the label using the chapter.
(c) The page has room for only three sites, and it must still show one example of each of the chapter's three major landforms. Which site should be dropped? Justify, using (a) and (b).
questions.a: (a) P is a plain (flat, no large hills or deep valleys, under 300 m); Q is a plateau (raised, more or less flat top, a steep side). (b) R is a hill, not a mountain: the chapter calls highlands with a lower height, less steep slopes and rounded tops hills; rising above the fields is true of hills and plateaus too. (c) Drop R. The three major landforms are mountains, plateaus and plains; P is the only plain, Q the only plateau and S the only site with a mountain's broad base, steep slopes and narrow summit. R is a hill, which the chapter treats as one of the 'other highlands', so dropping it loses no major landform, while dropping P, Q or S would.
s: (a) P plain and Q plateau, each matched to its shape
(b) R is a hill: lower height, less steep slopes, rounded top
(c) Drops R: P, Q and S are each the only example of plain, plateau and mountain, while R is a hill

questions.q: Asha, hiking at about 2,000 m, writes: 'The land stretches nearly flat for many kilometres, and at its edges steep cliffs drop to the country below.' Her friend says it must be a mountain because it is so high. Which reply uses the chapter correctly?
questions.a: It is a plateau: raised land whose surface is more or less flat
o: It is a plateau: raised land whose surface is more or less flat
It is a mountain: all land above about 1,000 m is mountain land
It is a plain: any flat land is a plain, whatever its height
It is a hill: highland without a narrow summit is a hill

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A highland about 600 m high, with gentle slopes and a rounded top, is called a hill and not a mountain.
Reason (R): A highland counts as a mountain only if its summit is permanently snow-capped.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. The altitude of a satellite and the altitude of a mountain are both measured from sea level.
2. A plain must be perfectly level; any gentle rise and fall in the land makes it a plateau.
3. A mountain and a plateau can both have steep slopes rising from the land around them.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A plateau's flat top stands 520 m above the plain at its foot, and that plain lies at the greatest height the chapter generally gives for plains. The plateau's top is ___ m above sea level.
Meera drives from Almora in Uttarakhand down to Prayagraj on the Ganga plain, then on to the Chhota Nagpur region in Jharkhand. Which set of field notes, in the order she writes them, fits her trip?
questions.a: steep slopes and narrow summits; wide flat land; raised land with a flat top
o: steep slopes and narrow summits; wide flat land; raised land with a flat top
wide flat land; steep slopes and narrow summits; raised land with a flat top
raised land with a flat top; wide flat land; steep slopes and narrow summits
steep slopes and narrow summits; raised land with a flat top; wide flat land

questions.q: At a Himalayan village, the snow on the slopes melts each May, but the snow on a peak above the village is still there in July. Which reason fits the chapter?
questions.a: The peak is at a higher altitude, where snow may never melt
o: The peak is at a higher altitude, where snow may never melt
The village slopes get hail, which melts much faster than snow
Snow on a peak is not precipitation, so it cannot melt
The peak has a flat top that shades and protects the snow

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column A with the term from the chapter that names it in Column B.
Column A: 1. Ladakh's winter snowfall and Kolkata's monsoon rain  2. A plane flying 9,000 m above the average level of the oceans  3. A rise of land with gentle slopes and a rounded top, far lower than the nearby peaks  4. A peak whose snow does not melt even in summer
Column B: a. altitude  b. precipitation  c. hill  d. permanently snow-capped
A quiz asks for a pair of places that belong to the SAME major landform. Which pair should be chosen?
questions.a: Flat land at 150 m and gently undulating farmland at 250 m
o: Flat land at 150 m and gently undulating farmland at 250 m
A raised flat-topped highland and a low, flat river floodplain
A narrow snowy summit and a flat-topped highland at 4,500 m
A low hill with a rounded top and a flat river floodplain

questions.q: A kite (bird) circles 500 m above a field, and the field itself is 200 m above sea level. (a) A student writes the bird's altitude as 500 m. What mistake has she made, and what is the correct altitude? (b) Is the field within the usual height of a plain?
questions.a: (a) She measured from the field, but altitude is the height above sea level; the bird is 200 + 500 = 700 m above sea level. (b) Yes: at 200 m the field is within the usual height of plains (generally not more than 300 m).
s: (a) Altitude is measured from sea level, so 700 m, not 500 m
(b) The field at 200 m is within the plain's usual limit of 300 m

questions.q: True or False? 'Any highland that rises above the land around it is a mountain.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. Rising above the surroundings is not enough. Hills also rise but have a lower height, less steep slopes and rounded tops, and plateaus rise but have a more or less flat top. A mountain has a broad base, steep slopes and a narrow summit.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: hills and plateaus also rise; a mountain needs steep slopes and a narrow summit

questions.q: Kavya lives in Chennai, a coastal city close to sea level, and has never seen snow, though her cousin in Sikkim sees it every winter. (a) Kavya says hail is just a kind of rain because both fall from clouds. In what way is hail more like snow than rain? (b) Why does snow fall in Sikkim but not in Chennai?
questions.a: (a) Hail and snow are both precipitation of water in a solid state, while rain is liquid water. (b) Snow falls at higher altitudes where it is cold enough; Sikkim is a Himalayan region at high altitude, while in Chennai, near sea level, precipitation comes as rain.
s: (a) Hail, like snow, is water falling in a solid state; rain is liquid
(b) Snow needs higher altitude and cold; Sikkim is Himalayan, Chennai is near sea level

questions.q: A drawing shows, at the back, two tall peaks with steep slopes, both white at the top. On the left is a raised block of land with a flat top and a steep edge. In the front is wide, flat land with a river that starts among the peaks at the back. (a) Name the landform in each of the three parts of the drawing. (b) A classmate says the land on the left and the land in front are the same landform because both are flat. Correct him using the drawing.
questions.a: (a) Back: mountains; left: plateau; front: plain. (b) Both are flat on top, but the land on the left rises up from the land around it with a steep edge, which makes it a plateau; the land in front is low, wide and flat, which makes it a plain.
s: (a) Mountains at the back, plateau on the left, plain in front
(b) The left block rises above its surroundings with a steep edge (plateau); the front land is low and flat (plain)

questions.q: Arjun says: 'A place 250 m above sea level must be on a plain, because plains are under 300 m.' Test his claim using the chapter.
questions.a: No. The 300 m figure says plains are GENERALLY not more than 300 m; it does not say that every low place is a plain. A plain is identified by its shape: an extensive flat or gently undulating surface without large hills or deep valleys. The chapter also says the height of plateaus can be as little as a few hundred metres, so a low raised block with a flat top could still be a plateau. Height must be read together with shape.
s: Verdict: the claim does not hold
A plain is defined by an extensive flat or gently undulating surface, not by height alone
Plateaus can be only a few hundred metres high, so height must be read with shape

questions.q: Write a three-line description of a place that a geographer would call a hill and not a mountain. Each line must give one feature, and after each line say which part of the chapter's rule it uses.
questions.a: Sample: 'It is much lower than the snowy peaks around it' (lower height than a mountain). 'Its sides rise gently and are easy to walk up' (less steep slopes). 'Its top is rounded, not a narrow point' (rounded top, unlike a mountain's narrow summit). Any three features matching lower height, less steep slopes and rounded top earn the marks.
s: A feature showing lower height, tied to the rule
A feature showing less steep slopes, tied to the rule
A feature showing a rounded top instead of a narrow summit

questions.q: A travel blogger writes after a trip from Prayagraj to Almora: 'The land just got higher, so I went from one landform to a taller version of the same one.' Give three different differences from the chapter (the top, the slopes, the height) that show he crossed two different landforms.
questions.a: 1. The top: the plain around Prayagraj is an extensive flat or gently undulating surface; the mountains near Almora end in a narrow summit. 2. The slopes: plains have no large hills or deep valleys; mountains have steep slopes and a broad base. 3. The height: plains are generally not more than 300 m above sea level; mountains are much higher than the surrounding landscape.
s: Top: extensive flat or undulating surface versus a narrow summit
Slopes: no large hills or deep valleys versus steep slopes and a broad base
Height: generally under 300 m versus much higher than the surroundings

questions.q: Justify the statement: 'To tell mountains, plateaus and plains apart, a geographer needs both height and shape; neither one is enough by itself.' Use at least two examples or figures from the chapter.
questions.a: Height alone fails: plateaus range from a few hundred metres to several thousand metres, so a high figure such as 4,500 m (the Tibetan Plateau's average altitude) can belong to a plateau, not only to a mountain; a height figure by itself cannot separate the two. Shape alone fails: a plain and a plateau can both be flat on top, and only height tells the raised plateau from a plain that is generally under 300 m. Together they work: a mountain is high with steep slopes and a narrow summit; a plateau rises from the land around it but keeps a more or less flat top; a plain is low (generally not more than 300 m) and flat or gently undulating. Hills show the same need: a hill is lower AND has rounded tops and less steep slopes.
s: Shows height alone fails, using the plateau height range or the 4,500 m Tibetan figure
Shows shape alone fails: plains and plateaus are both flat, height separates them
Concludes with the combined rule for all three landforms

questions.q: Design a two-question yes/no key that sorts any highland into 'mountain', 'hill' or 'plateau' using only the chapter's features. Then test it on these three places: X has a flat top 1,200 m high with one steep side; Y has a rounded top, gentle slopes and is much lower than nearby peaks; Z has a broad base, steep slopes and a narrow, snow-covered summit.
questions.a: Key: Q1 'Is the top broad and more or less flat?' Yes: plateau. No: go to Q2. Q2 'Does it have steep slopes and a narrow summit, much higher than its surroundings?' Yes: mountain. No (lower, less steep, rounded top): hill. Test: X has a flat top, so Q1 yes: plateau. Y: Q1 no, Q2 no (rounded, gentle, lower): hill. Z: Q1 no, Q2 yes: mountain.
s: First key question separates the flat-topped plateau
Second key question separates mountain (steep, narrow summit) from hill (lower, gentle, rounded)
X sorted correctly as plateau
Y sorted correctly as hill
Z sorted correctly as mountain

questions.q:
A farmer, Tenzing, lives in a village at about 1,800 m in Himachal Pradesh. He notes: snow covers his fields every winter and is gone by May; a monastery on the peak above, at about 5,200 m, is white all year; the stream below his village runs low in March and fills up in May and June. Lower down, in the plains, his brother says they get rain and hail but never snow, and he adds: 'Snow up in your mountains has nothing to do with the water we get down here.'
(a) Why does snow fall at Tenzing's village but not where his brother lives?
(b) Explain why the stream is fullest in May and June, while the snow near the monastery stays all year.
(c) Judge the brother's remark, using (b) and what the chapter says about rivers that start in mountains.
questions.a: (a) Snow falls at higher altitudes when it is cold enough; the village is high in a Himalayan region, while the plains are low, so precipitation there comes as rain and hail. (b) At lower altitudes the snow melts every summer and turns into water that feeds rivers and streams; at high altitudes, like the monastery's peak, the snow may never melt, leaving it permanently snow-capped. (c) The remark is wrong. Melting snow feeds rivers, and rivers that start in mountain ranges flow down to the plains (the Ganga, the largest river from the Himalayas, is one); they also carry sediments that they deposit on the plains, making the soil very fertile. So mountain snow does reach the plains as river water.
s: (a) Altitude and cold decide snowfall; the plains get rain and hail
(b) Summer melting at lower altitudes feeds the stream; at high altitude snow may never melt
(c) Rejects the remark: snowmelt feeds rivers that flow from the mountains down to the plains

questions.q: The chapter says humans have adapted to all landforms, but the number of people living on each kind varies. (a) A student guesses that more people live on plains simply because plains are low. Give the reason the chapter itself supports instead. (b) Why does the steepness of mountain land widen the gap?
questions.a: (a) Floodplains have very fertile soil from the sediments that rivers deposit, so they are ideal for growing crops of all kinds and agriculture can support many people. (b) Mountain terrain is rugged with steep slopes, so regular farming is possible only in some valleys; far less land can be farmed, so fewer people can live off it.
s: (a) Fertile river-deposited soil makes plains ideal for crops, supporting many people
(b) Steep, rugged slopes allow regular farming only in some valleys

questions.q: For a project on montane forests, Ishita draws the trees with round, spreading crowns and large, flat leaves. (a) Correct her drawing using the chapter's description of conifers. (b) Name two conifer trees she could label in the corrected drawing.
questions.a: (a) Conifers grow tall and cone-shaped, with thin, pointed leaves, so the crowns should be narrow cones and the leaves needle-thin. (b) Any two of pine, fir, spruce and deodar.
s: (a) Tall, cone-shaped trees with thin, pointed leaves
(b) Two of pine, fir, spruce, deodar

questions.q:
Match each climber's goal in Column A with the mountain in Column B that meets it.
Column A: 1. the highest point of the range the chapter places in Europe  2. a summit that stands alone in eastern Africa  3. the highest mountain of south India  4. the highest point of the range the chapter places in South America
Column B: a. Aconcagua  b. Kilimanjaro  c. Anamudi  d. Mont Blanc
True or False? 'A trekker climbing high up a Himalayan mountain should expect the plant cover to change from tall trees to low plants.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Mountain slopes are often covered with montane forest of tall conifers such as pine, fir, spruce and deodar, but at higher altitudes the trees give way to grasses, mosses and lichen.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: montane conifer forest lower down gives way to grasses, mosses and lichen higher up

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Aconcagua and Mont Blanc are the two highest peaks of the same range, the Andes.
2. Mont Blanc lies in Western Europe, while Aconcagua lies in South America.
3. Conifer trees of montane forests are short and broad, with wide, flat leaves.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 only
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: In Kalidasa's poem Kumarasambhava, written at least 1,500 years ago, the Himalaya is the 'Lord of mountains' that 'stretches from the western to the eastern oceans', and its wind carries 'spray from descending Ganga, shaking the deodar trees'. (a) Which statement in the chapter about the LENGTH of mountain ranges does 'stretches from ocean to ocean' match? (b) Why does the poet connect the Ganga with the Himalaya? (c) What does the mention of deodar tell us about the forest on these slopes?
questions.a: (a) Some mountain ranges, such as the Himalayas, stretch for thousands of kilometres. (b) The Ganga is the largest river originating from the Himalayas. (c) Deodar is a conifer, so the slopes carry montane forest.
s: (a) Ranges can stretch for thousands of kilometres
(b) The Ganga originates from the Himalayas
(c) Deodar is a conifer of montane forests

questions.q: A film crew wants to show the variety of Himalayan wildlife but has no permit to enter the deep forests. Which plan still fits the chapter's account of where mountain fauna live?
questions.a: Film at the mountain rivers, lakes, grasslands and caves
o: Film at the mountain rivers, lakes, grasslands and caves
Wait on the plains for the animals to come down
Film only the bare summits, where most animals live
Give up, since mountain animals live only inside deep forests

questions.q: A boat trip runs the whole length of the Ganga except its last 640 km. Using the river's length given in the chapter, the trip is nearly ___ km long.

Kalidasa, who lived at least 1,500 years ago, already praised the Himalaya as the 'Lord of mountains'. A student says this proves the Himalayas cannot be the 'young' mountains the chapter describes. Which reply fits the chapter?
questions.a: 'Young' means formed recently in Earth's history: millions of years ago
o: 'Young' means formed recently in Earth's history: millions of years ago
'Young' means formed in the last few hundred years, long after Kalidasa
Kalidasa was writing about the Aravallis, not the Himalayas
'Young' only means the mountains are lower than old ones

questions.q:
A school club is building a display on 'Young and old mountains'. Its notes on two Indian ranges read:
Range K: tall, sharp peaks; surveyors' note: 'still gaining height while rivers and weather keep wearing it down'.
Range L: much shorter, rounded hills and mountains; note: 'worn down over a very long time'.
There is room for one sentence under Range K. Member 1 proposes: 'K is being worn down, so it is getting shorter.' Member 2 proposes: 'K is still growing in height.'
(a) Decide which range goes under the heading 'young mountains', giving the feature you used.
(b) Which range named in the chapter fits Range L, and what process gave it its shape?
(c) Which member's sentence does the chapter support? Decide, and explain how K can gain height even though it is being worn down.
questions.a: (a) Range K: tall, sharp peaks mark relatively young mountains. (b) The Aravalli Range; it is much older and has been rounded by erosion. (c) Member 2. Both notes about K are true, but the chapter says that in ranges like the Himalayas upliftment continues along with erosion, and that such mountains are still growing in height; so the upliftment keeps adding height while erosion wears the peaks.
s: (a) Range K, because of its tall, sharp peaks
(b) The Aravalli Range, rounded by erosion
(c) Member 2: upliftment continues alongside erosion, so K is still growing

questions.q: Ravi says: 'Kilimanjaro should not be called a mountain, because it is not part of any mountain range.' Test his claim.
questions.a: No. The chapter says MOST of the world's mountains are grouped in ranges, not all. A mountain is recognised by being much higher than the surrounding landscape, with a broad base, steep slopes and a narrow summit. The chapter itself calls Kilimanjaro, in eastern Africa, an isolated mountain that is not part of any range, so being alone does not stop it being a mountain.
s: Verdict: the claim fails
Only most mountains are in ranges; a mountain is defined by its height and shape
The chapter calls Kilimanjaro an isolated mountain

questions.q: A student says: 'The Ganga collects water from more than one mountain range, not only from the Himalayas.' Is her claim supported by the chapter? Give reasons.
questions.a: Yes. The Ganga itself originates from the Himalayas, and some of its tributaries, like the Yamuna and the Ghagara, also originate there. But other tributaries, like the Son (or Sone), originate from the Vindhya Range to the south of the Ganga plain. So through its tributaries the Ganga gets water from at least two ranges.
s: Verdict: supported
The Ganga, the Yamuna and the Ghagara originate in the Himalayas
The Son originates in the Vindhya Range, south of the Ganga plain

questions.q: (a) A student from Kerala writes: 'Anamudi is the highest mountain in India.' Correct her sentence using the chapter's exact claim about Anamudi. (b) Her friend corrects it instead to 'Everest is the highest mountain in India.' Why is that also wrong, going by the chapter?
questions.a: (a) Anamudi (Anai Peak), in Kerala, is the highest mountain in south India. (b) The chapter places Mount Everest between Tibet (China) and Nepal, so it is not in India at all, even though it is the highest mountain in the world.
s: (a) Anamudi is the highest mountain in south India
(b) Everest lies between Tibet (China) and Nepal, not in India

questions.q: Mount Everest is 8,848 m high and the Tibetan Plateau has an average altitude of 4,500 m. (a) How many metres higher than the plateau's average altitude is Everest's summit? (b) Both are very high. What feature, not height, makes one a mountain and the other a plateau?
questions.a: (a) 8,848 - 4,500 = 4,348 m. (b) Shape of the top: Everest is a mountain with steep slopes and a narrow summit, while a plateau has a broad, more or less flat surface.
s: (b) Narrow summit and steep slopes versus a broad, flat top

questions.q: A tourist poster reads: 'Kanchenjunga, the highest peak of the Himalayas, stands on the border of Tibet and Nepal.' Show that the poster cannot be correct, pointing out both errors, and rewrite it correctly.
questions.a: Error 1: the highest peak of the Himalayas is Mount Everest (8,848 m, the highest mountain in the world), not Kanchenjunga; the two are the range's two highest peaks. Error 2: Kanchenjunga lies between Nepal and the Indian state of Sikkim; it is Everest that lies between Tibet (China) and Nepal. Correct poster: 'Kanchenjunga, one of the two highest peaks of the Himalayas, stands between Nepal and Sikkim.'
s: Error 1: Everest, not Kanchenjunga, is the highest Himalayan peak
Error 2: Kanchenjunga is between Nepal and Sikkim; Everest is between Tibet and Nepal
A correct rewritten poster

questions.q: A quiz-setter wants a clue whose answer is Mont Blanc and cannot be Aconcagua or Everest. Which clue works, going by the chapter?
questions.a: The highest mountain of the Alps
o: The highest mountain of the Alps
The highest peak of its own range
A mountain that lies outside India
One of six mountains in the chapter

questions.q: (a) Differentiate between moss and lichen as the chapter describes them. (b) A trekker finds a crusty growth stuck fast to a bare boulder near a summit. Which of the two is it more likely to be, and why?
questions.a: (a) A moss is a small green plant without flowers or true roots, often spreading in a cushion-like cover; a lichen is a plant-like organism that generally clings to rocks, walls or trees. (b) A lichen, because lichens generally cling to rocks, while a moss spreads as a soft, cushion-like cover.
s: (a) Moss: small green plant, no flowers or true roots, cushion-like; lichen: plant-like organism clinging to rocks, walls or trees
(b) Lichen, because it clings to rocks

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Aconcagua is the highest peak of the Andes.
Reason (R): Most of the world's mountains are grouped in mountain ranges.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A tour company's brochure for a Himalayan trek promises four things: (1) a walk through a forest of pine and deodar on the lower slopes; (2) a chance to spot a snow leopard near a mountain cave; (3) a stop at a high lake where a peregrine falcon hunts; (4) a visit to the source of the Son, 'a Himalayan river like the Ganga'. Evaluate each promise against the chapter, and give an overall judgement on the brochure.
questions.a: (1) Fits: mountain slopes are often covered with montane forest of conifers such as pine and deodar. (2) Fits: caves in the mountains are among the homes of fauna, and the snow leopard is named among mountain animals. (3) Fits: lakes in the mountains are home to fauna, and the peregrine falcon is a mountain bird in the chapter. (4) Does not fit: the Son (or Sone) is a Ganga tributary that originates in the Vindhya Range, south of the Ganga plain, not in the Himalayas (the Yamuna or the Ghagara would fit). Judgement: three promises match the chapter's mountain environment, but the brochure needs one correction about the Son.
s: (1) Pine and deodar montane forest fits
(2) Snow leopard and caves fit
(3) Lake and peregrine falcon fit
(4) Rejected: the Son rises in the Vindhya Range
Overall judgement with the correction

questions.q:
A trekking group in Uttarakhand keeps a log. At 2,200 m: 'a thick forest of tall trees shaped like cones, with thin, needle-like leaves'. At 3,400 m: 'trees thinning out, plenty of dead branches on the ground'. At 4,600 m: 'very cold; low green cushions on the ground and a grey crust stuck to the stones'. The leader wants to camp as high as possible to shorten the summit day, but needs fallen wood for a fire.
(a) What does the chapter call the forest at 2,200 m, and which two of its trees could the group have seen?
(b) What does the chapter call the two kinds of growth logged at 4,600 m, and what has happened to the trees by that height?
(c) Should the leader camp at 3,400 m or at 4,600 m? Decide, using (b).
questions.a: (a) Montane forest; any two of pine, fir, spruce and deodar. (b) The cushions are mosses and the crust on the stones is lichen; at higher altitudes the trees give way to grasses, mosses and lichen, so there are no trees there. (c) At 3,400 m. It is the higher of the two camps that still has trees and fallen wood; at 4,600 m the trees have given way to mosses and lichen, so there would be no wood, even though the summit day would be shorter.
s: (a) Montane forest with two conifers named
(b) Mosses and lichen; trees have given way at that height
(c) Camps at 3,400 m: highest site that still has wood, as 4,600 m is above the trees

questions.q: Compare the Himalayas and the Aravalli Range, and analyse what their shapes tell us about their age. Cover their peaks, their height, what has worn them, whether they are still changing, and what 'young' means here.
questions.a: Peaks: the Himalayas have tall, sharp peaks; the Aravallis are shorter and rounded. Age: tall, sharp peaks mark relatively young mountains, formed recently in the Earth's history, though still millions of years ago; the Aravallis are much older. Erosion: the Aravallis have been rounded by erosion over a long time. Still changing: in the Himalayas both upliftment and erosion continue to this day, so they are still growing in height. So a sharp shape points to youth and a rounded shape to great age and long erosion.
s: Contrasts tall, sharp peaks with shorter, rounded ones
Explains 'young' as recent in Earth's history, still millions of years ago
Links the Aravallis' rounded shape to long erosion
States that upliftment and erosion continue in the Himalayas, which still grow
Concludes that shape is evidence of age

questions.q: A map-maker is drawing the six mountains featured in the chapter. She will draw a mountain standing alone only if the chapter itself describes it as part of no range. How many of the six will she draw standing alone?
questions.a: One: Kilimanjaro, which the chapter calls part of no range
o: One: Kilimanjaro, which the chapter calls part of no range
None: every mountain belongs to some range
Two: Kilimanjaro and Anamudi, both being far from the Himalayas
Three: every mountain outside the Himalayas

questions.q: Dorje's family has two plots in a mountain village: a strip of flat land on a valley floor beside a stream, and a steep hillside. On which plot will they need to cut steps before growing crops, and why?
questions.a: The hillside, since crops on steep slopes need steps cut into them
o: The hillside, since crops on steep slopes need steps cut into them
The valley, since streams in valleys keep washing flat fields away
Both plots, since no mountain land can be farmed without steps
Neither plot, since herding is the only mountain occupation

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In mountain areas, crops are often grown on steps cut into the hillside.
Reason (R): Mountain terrain is usually rugged with steep slopes, so regular farming is possible only in some valleys.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
A Himalayan village of 40 homestays is deciding its tourist policy for next year. Last year 9,000 visitors came and the village's springs, its only drinking water, ran dry for two weeks. Each visitor spends about Rs 500 in the village.
Plan X: no limit; about 15,000 visitors are expected.
Plan Y: a limit of 7,000 visitors, each paying an extra Rs 300 to a village fund; owners expect about 12 of the 40 homestays to stand empty for much of the season.
(a) Name the mountain occupation this village depends on, and two features of mountains that the chapter says attract visitors.
(b) Work out the village's total income from visitors under Plan X and under Plan Y.
(c) What warning does the chapter give about visitors, and how do last year's springs illustrate it?
(d) Which plan should the village choose? Weigh the cost of your choice, using (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) Tourism; the crisp mountain air and the scenic beauty (sports and pilgrimages also draw people). (b) X: 15,000 x Rs 500 = Rs 75,00,000 (Rs 75 lakh). Y: 7,000 x Rs 800 = Rs 56,00,000 (Rs 56 lakh). (c) An excessive inflow of visitors puts the fragile mountain environment under pressure; at 9,000 visitors the springs already failed. (d) Plan Y, accepting its cost: it earns Rs 19 lakh less and leaves about 12 homestays (30%) idle for much of the season. But Plan X would bring 15,000 visitors, far above the 9,000 at which the only drinking water ran out, so it risks the springs on which the whole village, and its tourism, depends. Plan Y keeps numbers below that level, and the fee keeps income fairly high.
s: (a) Tourism, with crisp air and scenic beauty
(b) Rs 75 lakh under X and Rs 56 lakh under Y
(c) Excessive visitors pressure the fragile environment, as the dry springs show
(d) Chooses Y, weighing Rs 19 lakh less and idle homestays against X exceeding the 9,000 at which the springs failed

questions.q: A Tibetan herder calls the world's highest mountain 'Chomolungma' and a Nepali guide calls it 'Sagarmatha'. Which conclusion can be drawn from the meanings of the two names?
questions.a: Both see the peak as a goddess, but the names mean different things
o: Both see the peak as a goddess, but the names mean different things
Both names mean 'Goddess of the Sky', only in two different languages
Only Tibetans revere the peak; 'Sagarmatha' is just a name used on maps
The two names belong to two different peaks of the same range

questions.q:
Read the statements about challenges of mountain life.
1. Heavy snowfall and cold weather are among the challenges of mountain life that the chapter shows.
2. An avalanche can be a sudden fall of rocks from a mountainside, not only of snow.
3. The chapter counts uncontrolled tourism among the challenges of mountain life, even though it is human-made.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1, 2 and 3
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: A quiz card reads: 'This Indian climber reached the top of Everest and then the highest peak of every continent, including Mount Vinson in Antarctica.' A student answers 'Bachendri Pal, because she was the first Indian woman on Everest.' Why is the answer wrong?
questions.a: The card describes Arunima Sinha, whom Pal trained
o: The card describes Arunima Sinha, whom Pal trained
Pal was not the first Indian woman on Everest; Sinha was
Vinson is in South America, so the card is mistaken
Pal reached Everest after Arunima Sinha, in 2013

questions.q:
Match each village report in Column A with the hazard in Column B.
Column A: 1. 'Snow and ice from the upper slope suddenly crashed down onto the path.'  2. 'After weeks of rain, a mass of earth and rock collapsed from the hillside onto the road.'  3. 'A sudden, violent rainstorm burst over the upper valley.'  4. 'An hour later, the small stream rose suddenly and swept away a footbridge.'
Column B: a. landslide  b. cloudburst  c. avalanche  d. flash flood
A climber's last camp on Mount Everest is at 7,950 m. Using the height the chapter gives for Everest, she still has ___ m to climb to the summit.
A mountain family has only a tiny terraced field but a large stretch of steep, grassy slope around their house. Which way of earning a living, preferred in many mountain regions, best uses this land?
questions.a: Herding, which many mountain regions prefer to farming
o: Herding, which many mountain regions prefer to farming
Regular farming, ploughing the steep slope like a plain
Mining, which the chapter calls the major mountain activity
River fishing, which the chapter calls the main mountain job

questions.q: (a) What feature of mountain land limits regular farming, according to the chapter? (b) Use your answer to (a) to explain why herding is the preferred occupation in many mountain regions.
questions.a: (a) The terrain is rugged with steep slopes, so regular farming is possible only in some valleys. (b) Since little land can be farmed in the regular way, people use the slopes to keep and graze animals instead; herding fits the land better than farming.
s: (a) Rugged terrain and steep slopes leave only some valleys for regular farming
(b) Herding uses the land that farming cannot, so it is preferred

questions.q: True or False? 'Pilgrims are a new kind of visitor to the mountains, who began coming only with modern tourism.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says that for many centuries people have travelled to the uplands for pilgrimages to holy sites; pilgrimage is far older than modern tourism.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: people have travelled to the uplands for pilgrimages for many centuries

questions.q: (a) A Jain pilgrim and a pilgrim who follows Bon are travelling to the same sacred peak in Tibet. Which peak is it? (b) A Hindu and a Buddhist on the same bus ask whether the peak matters in their faiths too. What should they be told, and what does this show about one mountain's place in different religions?
questions.a: (a) Mount Kailash. (b) Yes: Kailash is held sacred by followers of Hinduism and Buddhism as well as Jainism and Bon, an ancient Tibetan religion. One mountain can be revered by four different religions at once.
s: (a) Mount Kailash
(b) Sacred in Hinduism and Buddhism too: one peak revered by four religions

questions.q: The chapter's pictures of mountain challenges show heavy snowfall, cold weather, a landslide and uncontrolled tourism. (a) Sort these four into natural and human-made challenges. (b) Why is the human-made one described as hard to manage, given that tourism is also a source of income?
questions.a: (a) Natural: heavy snowfall, cold weather, landslide. Human-made: uncontrolled tourism. (b) Tourism brings income, but an excessive inflow of visitors puts the fragile mountain environment under pressure, so it is often difficult to find the right balance.
s: (a) Three natural, uncontrolled tourism human-made
(b) Income versus pressure on a fragile environment: a balance is hard to find

questions.q: (a) Using the chapter's meanings, how is a cloudburst different from a flash flood? (b) A village high in a valley reports a sudden, violent rainstorm. What should a village lower down beside the same stream prepare for, and why?
questions.a: (a) A cloudburst is a sudden violent rainstorm; a flash flood is a sudden local flood. The first is rain falling, the second is water rising on the ground. (b) A flash flood, because the chapter says flash floods are often caused by a cloudburst; the rain upstream can make the stream rise suddenly lower down.
s: (a) Cloudburst is a sudden violent rainstorm; flash flood is a sudden local flood
(b) Prepare for a flash flood, often caused by a cloudburst

questions.q: A hotel owner in a hill town says: 'Tourism is good for the mountains in every way; the more visitors, the better.' Test this claim.
questions.a: Partly right. Right: tourism is often an important source of income for mountain people, drawn by crisp air, scenery, sports and pilgrimages. Wrong: 'in every way' and 'the more the better' go too far; the chapter warns that an excessive inflow of visitors puts the fragile mountain environment under pressure and that the right balance is often difficult to find.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: tourism is an important source of income
Wrong part: excessive visitors pressure the fragile environment; balance is needed

questions.q: A travel agency in Himachal Pradesh wants three advertisement lines for its mountain tours: one about health and comfort, one about sport, one about faith. Write the three lines and, after each, name what in the chapter supports it.
questions.a: Sample: 'Breathe the crisp mountain air' (the chapter says crisp air and scenic beauty attract tourists). 'Ski, hike or paraglide on our slopes' (skiing, hiking, mountaineering and paragliding are mountain sports). 'Walk the pilgrim paths of centuries' (people have travelled to uplands for pilgrimages to holy sites for many centuries). Any three lines matching these three draws earn the marks.
s: A line on crisp air or scenery, with its basis
A line on a mountain sport the chapter names
A line on pilgrimages to holy sites over centuries

questions.q: Despite avalanches, landslides, cloudbursts and cold weather, many people still choose to live in the mountains. Interpret why, giving three different reasons from the chapter that do not depend on tourists.
questions.a: 1. Livelihoods that suit the land: regular farming in some valleys, terrace farming on the slopes and herding, which many mountain regions prefer. 2. The positives of mountain life itself: pure, crisp air and beautiful scenery. 3. Cultural and religious ties: many communities hold mountains sacred and worship them, as with Everest (Chomolungma, Sagarmatha) and Mount Kailash. These benefits make people adapt instead of leaving.
s: Livelihoods from valley and terrace farming and herding
Positives of pure air and beautiful scenery
Sacred and cultural ties to the mountains

questions.q: 'Life in the mountains has definite positives as well as potential challenges.' Compare the two sides and give a balanced judgement, using at least two positives, three challenges (both natural and human-made) and the role of tourism.
questions.a: Positives: pure, crisp air and beautiful scenery; tourism and pilgrimage income; herding and terrace farming that suit the land. Natural challenges: avalanches (often when snow starts melting), landslides, flash floods often caused by cloudbursts, heavy snowfall and cold weather; rugged terrain limits regular farming to some valleys. Human-made challenge: uncontrolled tourism. Tourism sits on both sides: it brings income but an excessive inflow puts the fragile environment under pressure. Judgement: the positives keep people in the mountains, but living there needs adaptation and a careful balance, especially in tourism.
s: Two positives of mountain life
Three natural challenges named correctly
The human-made challenge of uncontrolled tourism
Tourism shown as both income and pressure
A balanced judgement about adapting and finding balance

questions.q: Compare and analyse the mountaineering lives of Bachendri Pal and Arunima Sinha using the chapter. Work out (i) how many years apart they climbed Everest, (ii) how long after her Everest climb each received the Padma Shri, and (iii) how many years separate Pal's two Padma awards. Then explain how the two women's stories are linked, and judge which fact best shows that a serious setback need not end a climber's ambitions.
questions.a: (i) Pal climbed Everest in 1984 and Sinha in 2013: 2013 - 1984 = 29 years apart. (ii) Pal received the Padma Shri in 1984, the same year as her climb (0 years); Sinha received it in 2015, 2015 - 2013 = 2 years after hers. (iii) Pal's Padma Shri (1984) and Padma Bhushan (2019) are 2019 - 1984 = 35 years apart. Link: Pal, the first Indian woman on Everest, who also led many women's expeditions, encouraged and trained Sinha. Judgement: Sinha lost a leg in an accident at 22, yet climbed Everest and went on to climb the highest peak of every continent, including Mount Vinson in Antarctica; this best shows that a setback need not end a climber's ambitions.
s: (i) 29 years between the Everest climbs
(ii) Padma Shri 0 years after for Pal, 2 years after for Sinha
(iii) 35 years between Pal's Padma Shri and Padma Bhushan
Link: Pal encouraged and trained Sinha
Judgement using Sinha's lost leg and her later climbs

questions.q:
A district has one rescue team to station for the month of April. Two villages ask for it.
Village B: 600 people in a narrow valley beside a stream; its past flash floods all came in July and August.
Village C: 150 people in houses below a steep slope that holds deep snow all winter and starts to thaw in April.
(a) Name the hazard that most threatens Village C, and say what it is.
(b) Why is April a likely time for that hazard at Village C?
(c) Village B has four times as many people. Where should the team be stationed for April? Decide, using (a) and (b).
questions.a: (a) An avalanche: the sudden fall of snow, ice or rocks from a mountainside. (b) The chapter says avalanches often occur when the snow starts melting, and C's slope starts to thaw in April. (c) Village C for April. B is larger (600 is four times 150), but its flash floods have come in July and August, not April, while April is exactly when C's snow starts melting and avalanches often occur. The team can be moved to B before the July-August flood season.
s: (a) Avalanche, a sudden fall of snow, ice or rocks
(b) Avalanches often occur when the snow starts melting, as C's does in April
(c) Chooses C for April, weighing B's larger population against the timing of each hazard

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. The Victoria Falls are on the Sharavati River in the Western Ghats.
2. Lava plateaus are an exception to the rule that plateau soil is generally less fertile than that of plains.
3. The Deccan Plateau was formed through volcanic activity and is one of the oldest plateaus in the world.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Explain, using the chapter's examples, why mining rather than farming is the major activity on many plateaus. Give three points.
questions.a: 1. Plateaus are rich in mineral deposits and have been called storehouses of minerals, so many of the world's largest mines are on them. 2. Examples: the East African Plateau for gold and diamonds; the Chhota Nagpur Plateau for iron, coal and manganese. 3. Many plateaus have rocky soil, less fertile than plains, so they are less favourable to farming (lava plateaus with black soil are the exception).
s: Plateaus are storehouses of minerals with many of the largest mines
Examples from East Africa and Chhota Nagpur with their minerals
Rocky soil makes farming less favourable, lava plateaus excepted

questions.q: The answer to a quiz question is 'the Chhota Nagpur Plateau'. Write three different clues, each based on the chapter, any one of which would point to this answer and not to the Deccan Plateau.
questions.a: Sample clues: 1. 'Huge reserves of iron, coal and manganese are found here.' 2. 'The Hundru Falls on the Subarnarekha River drop from it.' 3. 'A road journey that starts here in Jharkhand and goes on to Prayagraj and Almora crosses all three major landforms.' (The Deccan is instead one of the oldest plateaus, formed through volcanic activity, in central and south India.)
s: Clue on iron, coal and manganese reserves
Clue on the Hundru Falls and the Subarnarekha River
Clue on its place in Jharkhand or the chapter's opening journey

questions.q: Neha writes: 'Plateaus are just low hills with flat tops.' Test her claim using the chapter.
questions.a: No. Plateaus need not be low: their heights range from a few hundred metres to several thousand metres, and the Tibetan Plateau averages 4,500 m. Hills have rounded tops and less steep slopes, while a plateau has a broad, more or less flat surface with some steep sides. A plateau is one of the three main types of landform, not a kind of hill.
s: Verdict: the claim fails
Plateaus can be thousands of metres high, as the Tibetan Plateau shows
Hills have rounded tops; a plateau has a flat surface and is a main landform of its own

questions.q: The chapter twice compares plateaus with mountains, using the words 'like mountains'. (a) State the two ways in which plateaus are like mountains. (b) State one way in which a plateau's shape differs from a mountain's.
questions.a: (a) Like mountains, plateaus can be young or old in the Earth's history, and like mountains they are rich in mineral deposits. (b) A plateau has a broad, more or less flat surface, while a mountain has a narrow summit.
s: (a) Both can be young or old, and both are rich in minerals
(b) Flat top versus narrow summit

questions.q: Justify the statement: 'India's plateaus matter to its people in more than one way.' Use at least three Indian plateaus or plateau regions named in the chapter and three different kinds of value.
questions.a: Minerals: the Chhota Nagpur Plateau holds huge reserves of iron, coal and manganese, so mining is a major activity. Soil: the Deccan Plateau, one of the world's oldest, was formed through volcanic activity, which makes it a lava plateau by the chapter's definition, and lava plateaus often have rich black soil, an exception to the rocky soil of most plateaus. Waterfalls: the Hundru Falls on the Subarnarekha (Chhota Nagpur), the Jog Falls on the Sharavati (Western Ghats) and the Nohkalikai Falls dropping 340 m from the Cherrapunji Plateau show plateaus are home to spectacular waterfalls. So plateaus give minerals, sometimes fertile soil and striking landscapes.
s: Mineral value with Chhota Nagpur's iron, coal and manganese
Soil value: Deccan's volcanic origin makes it a lava plateau, which often has rich black soil
Waterfalls with correct plateau or river
A third plateau or region correctly used
Conclusion that the value is many-sided

questions.q: Geologists report huge reserves of iron ore and coal in a plateau region of Jharkhand. A student says this is surprising, because minerals belong in mountains. Which reply fits the chapter?
questions.a: Not surprising: plateaus too are 'storehouses of minerals'
o: Not surprising: plateaus too are 'storehouses of minerals'
Surprising: rocky plateau soil means a plateau has no minerals
Not surprising: river sediments carry iron and coal up to plateaus
Surprising: only plateaus abroad, such as East Africa, hold minerals

questions.q: A planning team compares three kinds of land for two uses, crop farming and mining: a lava plateau, a rocky plateau rich in minerals, and a river floodplain. Using only what the chapter says, (i) name the land that is poorest for farming, (ii) name the best land for mining, and (iii) explain why both the lava plateau and the floodplain can be good for crops, even though their fertile soil comes about in different ways. Justify every choice.
questions.a: (i) The rocky plateau: many plateaus have a rocky soil, which makes them less fertile than plains and less favourable to farming. (ii) The rocky, mineral-rich plateau: plateaus are rich in mineral deposits, 'storehouses of minerals', and many of the world's largest mines are on them, as in the Chhota Nagpur Plateau (iron, coal, manganese) or the East African Plateau (gold, diamonds). (iii) The lava plateau is formed through volcanic activity and is the chapter's exception among plateaus, because lava plateaus often have a rich black soil. The floodplain is made very fertile by sediments of rock, sand and silt that rivers bring down from the mountains and deposit, so it is ideal for crops of all kinds. One fertile soil comes from volcanic activity, the other from river sediments. So the same rocky plateau can be poor for crops but valuable for minerals.
s: (i) Rocky plateau poorest for farming, because rocky soil is less fertile
(ii) Mineral-rich plateau best for mining, with the storehouse reason
(iii) Lava plateau fertile because of its rich black soil from volcanic activity
(iii) Floodplain fertile because rivers deposit sediments there
Contrasts the two origins of fertile soil and concludes

questions.q:
Match each surveyor's note about a plateau in Column A with what the chapter would say about it in Column B.
Column A: 1. thin, stony soil with seams of coal and iron  2. land built up by volcanic activity long ago  3. a river crossing the flat top drops over a steep edge  4. a vast flat upland averaging 4,500 m
Column B: a. likely to have a rich black soil  b. the 'Roof of the World'  c. mining is likely to be a major activity  d. a waterfall, a feature many plateaus are home to
Four students each write one line for a plateau fact-check board. Which line passes the check against the chapter?
questions.a: A plateau may have steep slopes on some sides
o: A plateau may have steep slopes on some sides
Every plateau is lower than every mountain
Plateau soil is always more fertile than plain soil
Waterfalls form on mountains, but never on plateaus

questions.q: A travel vlogger in Meghalaya films a river crossing a flat tableland and then plunging over its steep edge. Which description fits what she is filming, going by the chapter?
questions.a: Nohkalikai Falls, dropping 340 m from the Cherrapunji Plateau
o: Nohkalikai Falls, dropping 340 m from the Cherrapunji Plateau
Jog Falls, dropping from the Sharavati plateau inside Meghalaya
Hundru Falls, on the Subarnarekha River close to Cherrapunji
Victoria Falls, on the Zambezi where it leaves Meghalaya

questions.q: (a) The chapter never uses the words 'lava plateau' for the Deccan Plateau. Which fact it gives about the Deccan lets you call it one? (b) Using what the chapter says about lava plateaus, explain why a farmer on parts of the Deccan might find richer soil than a farmer on a rocky plateau.
questions.a: (a) The Deccan was formed through volcanic activity millions of years ago, and the chapter defines lava plateaus as plateaus formed through volcanic activity. (b) Lava plateaus often have rich black soil, while many plateaus have rocky, less fertile soil; so volcanic land like the Deccan can carry better soil for crops (the chapter says 'often', not always).
s: (a) The Deccan was formed through volcanic activity, which is what defines a lava plateau
(b) Lava plateaus often have rich black soil, unlike rocky plateaus

questions.q:
A survey team reports on three sites on an Indian plateau.
Site R: soil thin and stony; test pits show seams of coal and iron ore.
Site S: soil deep and dark; the rocks show the land was built up by volcanic activity long ago; the nearest stream is 3 km away.
Site T: soil thin and stony; no minerals found; a river runs right beside it and falls over the plateau's steep edge.
A mining company is given Site R. A farming cooperative must choose between S and T.
(a) What kind of plateau does the chapter call land like Site S, and what does it say about such land's soil?
(b) Why does the chapter make Site R a sensible choice for the mining company?
(c) The cooperative's secretary prefers T because the river is right beside it. Should the cooperative choose S or T? Decide, weighing water against soil.
questions.a: (a) A lava plateau (formed through volcanic activity), which often has a rich black soil, the chapter's exception to plateau soil being less fertile than plains. (b) Plateaus are rich in mineral deposits ('storehouses of minerals') and mining is a major activity on them; R's coal and iron are like the Chhota Nagpur Plateau's reserves, and its stony soil is poor for crops anyway. (c) Site S. T has water close by, but its thin, stony soil is the rocky plateau soil the chapter calls less fertile and less favourable to farming; S has the rich black soil of a lava plateau. Water can be brought 3 km, but poor soil cannot easily be changed, so S is the better choice despite the distance.
s: (a) Lava plateau, often with rich black soil
(b) Plateaus are storehouses of minerals and mining is major on them
(c) Chooses S, weighing T's nearby water against its rocky, less fertile soil

questions.q: A fact-checker reviews four plateau labels for a school exhibition. Which label should she REJECT, going by the chapter?
questions.a: Deccan Plateau: famous for its gold and diamond mines
o: Deccan Plateau: famous for its gold and diamond mines
Cherrapunji Plateau: source of the Nohkalikai Falls
Tibetan Plateau: an average altitude of about 4,500 m
Chhota Nagpur Plateau: home of the Hundru Falls

questions.q: A bus crosses the Tibetan Plateau from east to west, covering 250 km a day. Using the plateau's east-west length given in the chapter, the crossing takes about ___ days.

(a) Differentiate between a plateau and a plain, giving one Indian example of each from the chapter. (b) A survey finds land 900 m above sea level with a more or less flat surface and a steep slope on one side. Using (a), which landform is it, and which TWO features decide it?
questions.a: (a) A plateau rises up from the surrounding land and has a more or less flat surface, often with steep slopes on some sides (the Deccan or Chhota Nagpur Plateau); a plain is an extensive flat or gently undulating surface, generally not more than 300 m above sea level (the Ganga plain). (b) A plateau: it is far above the 300 m that plains generally do not exceed, and its steep side shows it rises above the land around it while its top stays flat.
s: (a) Plateau raised with a flat top versus plain low and flat, with an example of each
(b) Plateau, decided by its height above 300 m and its steep side with a flat top

questions.q: A drawing shows, on the left, a raised block of land with a flat top and a steep cliff on its right side. A river flows across the flat top and drops straight down the cliff. On the right is low, flat land. (a) Name the landform on the left and the feature where the river drops. (b) The chapter gives such a feature on the Chhota Nagpur Plateau. Name it and the river it is on.
questions.a: (a) A plateau (raised, flat top, steep side) and a waterfall. (b) The Hundru Falls, on the Subarnarekha River.
s: (a) Plateau and waterfall
(b) Hundru Falls on the Subarnarekha River

questions.q:
A travel-diary entry reads: 'Our bus climbed steeply for two days. Then the land flattened into a wide, high tableland that seemed endless. The air was thin; the guide said we were about 4,500 m above sea level on average, on the largest and highest land of its kind in the world.' Two classmates disagree about the title of the class report. Ravi wants 'The highest plain in the world', because the land was flat and endless. Meena wants 'The Roof of the World: a plateau'.
(a) Name the land the diary describes.
(b) Why did the land 'flatten' though it was so high? Use the definition of this landform.
(c) How many metres higher is its average altitude than the height plains generally do not exceed?
(d) Ravi's point about flatness is true. Whose title should the report use? Decide, using (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) The Tibetan Plateau. (b) A plateau rises up from the surrounding land but has a more or less flat surface, so after the steep climb the top is flat. (c) 4,500 - 300 = 4,200 m. (d) Meena's. Ravi is right that the surface is flat, but a flat surface is shared by plains and plateaus; what separates them is that this land rose steeply from the land around it and stands about 4,200 m above the height plains generally do not exceed. That makes it a plateau, nicknamed the 'Roof of the World'.
s: (a) Tibetan Plateau
(b) A plateau rises from the land around it but has a flat top
(d) Chooses Meena's title: flatness is shared, but the steep rise and the 4,200 m gap make it a plateau

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Most plateaus are better for farming than plains, because plateaus are rich in minerals.
Reason (R): Plateaus have been called 'storehouses of minerals'.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: True or False? 'A flat-topped upland that rises only about 400 m above sea level can still be a plateau.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. A plateau is identified by rising from the surrounding land with a more or less flat surface, and the chapter says plateau heights vary from a few hundred metres to several thousand metres, so 400 m is within that range.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: plateaus are known by a raised, flat top and can be only a few hundred metres high

questions.q: A news headline says: 'Irrigation has been a blessing for the Ganga plain.' Test this claim using the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. Right: in recent decades farming turned from rainfed to irrigated, with water from canals or pumped from groundwater, and this has increased agricultural production. Wrong to call it only a blessing: irrigation has also contributed to the depletion of groundwater, which the chapter calls a challenge for the future of agriculture in the region.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: irrigation has increased production
Missing part: groundwater depletion threatens future farming

questions.q:
Read this account of a fair in the Ganga plain.
'Every winter, lakhs of people gather where a smaller river meets the Ganga. Boatmen ferry pilgrims across the wide water from dawn to dusk. Along the bank, farmers from nearby villages set up stalls selling rice, jute rope, wheat flour and cotton cloth.'
This year the ground at the river bank is crowded, and a committee member proposes moving the fair 20 km away to a large, empty field with no river, where there is far more room.
(a) What does the chapter call the place where the fair is held, and why do communities treat such places as special?
(b) Why, according to the chapter, are the plains around the fair so good for growing the rice and wheat sold there?
(c) Sort the goods on sale by the crop each comes from: which are food crops and which are fibre crops?
(d) Should the fair move to the empty field? Weigh the extra space against what (a) and the boatmen's work show, and decide.
questions.a: (a) A confluence, the meeting point of two or more rivers; many communities consider a river's confluence sacred, and festivals, ceremonies and rituals are held there. (b) Rivers from the mountains carry sediments (rock, sand and silt) and deposit them on the plains, making the soil very fertile and ideal for crops of all kinds. (c) Food crops: rice and wheat. Fibre crops: jute and cotton. (d) It should not move. The field gives more room, but the fair's sacred reason exists only at the confluence, and the boatmen's work depends on the river, which in the plains is easy to navigate because of the gentle slope; at a field with no river both are lost. Crowding is better handled at the site itself.
s: (a) A confluence, regarded as sacred
(b) River-deposited sediments make the plain's soil very fertile
(c) Rice and wheat food crops; jute and cotton fibre crops
(d) Decides to stay, weighing space against the sacred confluence and river transport

questions.q:
A village in the Ganga plain used to grow its crops on rainfall alone. Over the last twenty years it turned to tube-wells that pump groundwater onto the fields. Village records:
2005: water found 8 m below the ground; wheat 25 quintals per hectare.
2025: water found 20 m below the ground; wheat 40 quintals per hectare.
The village's hand pumps, its drinking water, stop working if the water falls below 25 m. The panchayat must choose: Plan W, drill 10 more tube-wells, which experts say would double the yearly fall; Plan C, drill no new tube-wells and bring water through the canal network, which reaches the village only in some months, so wheat is expected to drop to about 34 quintals per hectare.
(a) Which change in farming described in the chapter explains the rise in wheat yield?
(b) By how many metres per year, on average, did the water level fall from 2005 to 2025?
(c) At that rate, in about how many years will the hand pumps stop, and in about how many years under Plan W?
(d) Which option should the panchayat choose? Weigh the cost of your choice, using (b), (c) and the challenge the chapter names.
questions.a: (a) The shift from rainfed farming to irrigation, with water pumped from groundwater, which has increased agricultural production. (b) (20 - 8) / 20 = 0.6 m per year. (c) (25 - 20) / 0.6 = about 8 years; at double the rate, 1.2 m per year, about 4 years. (d) Plan C, accepting its cost: wheat falls from 40 to about 34 quintals per hectare (a 15% drop) because canal water comes only in some months. But the chapter warns that irrigation from groundwater has contributed to its depletion, a challenge for the future of agriculture; Plan W would halve the time before the drinking-water hand pumps fail, to about 4 years, after which the tube-wells too would be pumping from an ever lower level. A smaller harvest is the safer loss.
s: (a) Rainfed farming replaced by irrigation from groundwater
(b) 0.6 m per year
(c) About 8 years now, about 4 years under Plan W
(d) Chooses Plan C, weighing the 15% lower yield against faster groundwater depletion

questions.q: (a) Name the two places on a river that the chapter says many communities consider sacred. (b) The chapter brings these up while describing plains, though it says rivers have cultural value 'whether in mountain ranges or plains'. Using the Ganga, show why the mountains and the plains both share in this.
questions.a: (a) A river's source and its confluence with one or two other rivers. (b) The Ganga originates from the Himalayas, so its source lies in the mountains; it then flows across the Ganga plain, where tributaries join it at confluences, and in India festivals, ceremonies and rituals are held at such places. So the river's sacred places are spread across both landforms.
s: (a) The source and the confluence
(b) Source in the Himalayas, confluences on the plain: both landforms share the river's sacred places

questions.q: Compare life in the Ganga plain 'in earlier days' with life 'in our times', and analyse what has changed and what has stayed the same. Cover where people settled, how fields were watered, how rivers were used for travel, and the new problems of today. End with a judgement on whether the river still matters as much as it once did.
questions.a: Settlement: thousands of years ago the first civilisations developed around rivers in fertile plains; today a large part of the world's population lives in plains, and the Ganga plain holds more than one-fourth of India's people (same). Watering: traditional agriculture was mostly rainfed; in recent decades it has turned to irrigation through canals or pumped groundwater, which has increased production (changed). Travel: in earlier days people used rivers extensively to travel; even today there are stretches of the Ganga where people prefer boats, since the gentle slope makes navigation easy (partly the same). New problems: groundwater depletion from irrigation, high population and pollution. Judgement: the river still matters as much, for soil, water, travel and sacred confluences, but people now draw on it harder, which brings new pressures.
s: Settlement then and now: first civilisations and today's large population
Rainfed farming replaced by irrigation, raising production
River travel then and the boats still used today
Today's problems: groundwater depletion, high population, pollution
A judgement on the river's importance with the new pressures

questions.q: A grandfather in Bihar says his crops once 'waited for the sky'; his grandson's crops now get water from a pump in the field. Which change does this show, and what risk does the chapter link to it?
questions.a: Rainfed to irrigated farming, risking groundwater depletion
o: Rainfed to irrigated farming, risking groundwater depletion
Irrigated to rainfed farming, with a risk of yearly drought
Farming to river fishing, with a risk of more pollution
Canal water to rainfall, risking a higher population

questions.q: Two students argue about plains and floodplains. Which statement settles the argument correctly?
questions.a: Floodplains are one type of plain; not every plain is one
o: Floodplains are one type of plain; not every plain is one
Every plain is a floodplain, as all plains are made by rivers
Floodplains lie above 300 m; all other plains lie below it
Floodplains are made from sediments the sea leaves behind

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Ganga plain.
1. Floodplains are formed by rivers that begin in mountain ranges.
2. Since irrigation spread, the level of groundwater has been rising.
3. The chapter says the only problem facing the Ganga plains is groundwater depletion.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 only
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Match each feature of the Ganga plain in Column A with its cause in Column B, as the chapter gives it.
Column A: 1. groundwater depletion  2. very fertile soil  3. easy river navigation  4. festivals at certain river spots
Column B: a. sediments deposited by rivers from the mountains  b. confluences regarded as sacred  c. water pumped up for irrigation  d. the gentle slope of the land

Assertion (A): River navigation is easy across the Ganga plain.
Reason (R): The soil of the Ganga plain is fertile because rivers deposit sediments there.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: True or False? 'A river can make farmland fertile hundreds of kilometres away from the mountains where it begins.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Rivers that begin in mountain ranges collect sediments (rock, sand and silt) and carry them all the way to the plains, where they deposit them and make the soil very fertile.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: rivers carry sediments from the mountains all the way to the plains and deposit them

questions.q: Interpret why plains have drawn people from the time of the first civilisations to the present. Give three reasons from the chapter, each tied to a different feature of a river plain.
questions.a: 1. Fertile soil: rivers deposit sediments that make the soil very fertile, ideal for crops of all kinds, so agriculture is a major occupation that can feed many people. 2. Food from the river itself: river fishing is one of the major occupations in plains such as the Ganga plain. 3. Easy movement: plains have a gentle slope, so river navigation is easy and supports a lot of economic activity and travel. That is why the first civilisations developed around rivers in fertile plains and a large part of the world's population lives in plains today.
s: Fertile river-deposited soil supports agriculture
River fishing as a further livelihood
Gentle slope makes navigation easy, supporting economic activity

questions.q: (a) A news report lists the problems of the Ganga plains as 'landslides and avalanches'. Replace these with the two problems the chapter names besides groundwater depletion. (b) Link one of your two problems to the plain's fertile soil.
questions.a: (a) High population and pollution (landslides and avalanches are hazards of mountain life). (b) The fertile soil supports agriculture and river fishing, so a very large number of people live there, which leads to high population.
s: (a) High population and pollution, not mountain hazards
(b) Fertile land supports many livelihoods, so population is high

questions.q: About 40 crore people live in the Ganga plain, and the chapter says this is more than one-fourth of India's population. So India's population must be less than ___ crore.

(a) Suppose India's population is taken as 140 crore. Using the chapter's figure for the Ganga plain, what fraction of India's people live there, and does it fit the chapter's words 'more than one-fourth'? (b) A student concludes, 'So most Indians live in the Ganga plain.' Is this a correct reading? Explain.
questions.a: (a) 40/140 = 2/7, about 0.29 (29%), which is more than one-fourth (0.25), so it fits. (b) No. 'Most' means more than half; about 2/7 is well under half, so most Indians live outside the Ganga plain.
s: (a) 40/140 = 2/7, about 29%, more than one-fourth
(b) More than one-fourth is not most (over half)

questions.q: (a) A village on a stretch of the Ganga has a good road, yet many people still go to market by boat. Is this unusual, according to the chapter? (b) Which feature of plains makes river travel easy there?
questions.a: (a) No. In earlier days people used rivers extensively to travel from one place to another, and even today there are stretches along the Ganga where people prefer to use boats to move around. (b) Plains have a gentle slope, so river navigation is easy.
s: (a) Not unusual: rivers were used for travel and boats are still preferred on some stretches
(b) The gentle slope of plains makes navigation easy

questions.q: After the river flooded, a farmer in Bihar found a fresh layer of silt on her field, and her next crop grew better than before. Which explanation fits the chapter?
questions.a: The river laid down sediments it had carried down from the mountains
o: The river laid down sediments it had carried down from the mountains
The flood water washed minerals off a nearby plateau onto her fields
The silt was carried in from the sea at high tide by the river water
The flood lowered the field below 300 m, which made it fertile

questions.q: A brochure describes a region as 'a plain about 1,200 m above sea level, broken by large hills and deep valleys'. Show, with three reasons from the chapter's definition, that this cannot be a plain.
questions.a: 1. Plains are generally not more than 300 m above sea level; 1,200 m is four times that, so the height alone makes a plain very unlikely (the 300 m is a general figure, so the next two reasons settle it). 2. Plains do not have any large hills. 3. Plains do not have deep valleys; their surface is extensive and flat or gently undulating. Reasons 2 and 3 are part of what a plain is, so a land 'broken by large hills and deep valleys' cannot be a plain.
s: Height: plains are generally under 300 m, not 1,200 m
Plains have no large hills
Plains have no deep valleys; they are flat or gently undulating, so the surface rules it out

questions.q: A surveyor writes four notes. Which note describes a plain?
questions.a: Extensive, gently undulating land at 180 m with no deep valleys
o: Extensive, gently undulating land at 180 m with no deep valleys
Flat-topped land at 180 m that rises steeply from its surroundings
Wide, flat land at 900 m, cut through by deep river valleys
Gently rolling land at 250 m, broken by several large hills

questions.q: Compare life on the plains with life in the mountains on four points: how crops are grown, the other main occupations, one major challenge of each, and what each holds sacred. Then judge which landform the chapter suggests supports more people, and why.
questions.a: Crops: plains have fertile river-deposited soil ideal for crops of all kinds; in mountains regular farming is possible only in some valleys, and slopes need terrace farming. Occupations: plains have river fishing and agriculture; mountains have herding (often preferred) and tourism. Challenges: plains face groundwater depletion (also high population and pollution); mountains face avalanches, landslides, flash floods and cloudbursts. Sacred: in plains, river sources and confluences; in mountains, summits such as Everest (Chomolungma, Sagarmatha) and Kailash. Judgement: plains support more people, since fertile soil and easy farming mean a large part of the world's population lives in plains, while rugged mountain land can be farmed only in places.
s: Crops: fertile plains versus valleys and terraces
Occupations: fishing and farming versus herding and tourism
A correct challenge for each landform
Sacred confluences versus sacred summits
Judges that plains support more people, with the reason

questions.q:
Read the statements about the five tinais.
1. The tinais group land by landscape and link each landscape to a main occupation.
2. The tinais include a coastal landscape, which the chapter's three main landforms do not list as a separate type.
3. The tinais are simply the three main landforms with Tamil names.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only
o: 1 and 2 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Priya says: 'The tinais show that ancient Tamil poets understood that the kind of land people live on shapes the work they do.' Is her claim supported by the chapter?
questions.a: Yes. The tinai table pairs every landscape with a main occupation: mountains with hunting and gathering, grassland and forests with cattle rearing, fertile plains with farming, coasts with fishing and seafaring, and arid land with journeying and fighting. The chapter says the tinais reflect a keen awareness of diverse regions and the deep connection between humanity and the natural environment.
s: Verdict: supported
Evidence: each tinai landscape is paired with its occupation
The chapter's own words on awareness of regions and the human-nature link

questions.q: (a) Which tinai matches the chapter's mountains, and which matches its plains? (b) Which tinai fits the extra landform the chapter adds at the end? (c) Name one tinai landscape that is none of these four landforms.
questions.a: (a) Kurinji (mountainous regions) matches mountains; Marudam (fertile agricultural plains) matches plains. (b) Palai, the arid, desert-like region, fits deserts. (c) Neydal (coastal regions) or Mullai (grassland and forests).
s: (a) Kurinji with mountains, Marudam with plains
(b) Palai with deserts
(c) Neydal or Mullai named as outside these four

questions.q: Compare the chapter's three main landforms with the five tinais of Tamil Sangam poetry, and analyse what each classification helps us understand. Cover their basis, their number of types, one landscape found in one scheme but not the other, and what each shows about people and land.
questions.a: Basis: the three main landforms are told apart by height and shape (narrow summit, flat top, low flat land); the tinais are told apart by landscape and the main occupation in each. Number: three versus five. Difference: the tinais include coastal regions (Neydal), grassland and forests (Mullai) and arid land (Palai), which are not among the three main landforms; the three-landform scheme has plateaus, which no tinai names. What each shows: the landforms scheme describes the physical surface and its environments; the tinais show a keen awareness of regions and how landscape shapes human work, the deep link between humanity and nature. Judgement: they answer different questions, so both are useful.
s: Basis: height and shape versus landscape and occupation
Three types versus five
A landscape in one scheme but not the other, such as coast or plateau
What each scheme shows about land and people
Judgement that both are useful for different purposes

questions.q: At a school festival, a folk singer from a Thar village sings old songs about sand, wells and long journeys. Which idea from the chapter does this best show?
questions.a: Desert communities hold rich traditions about the desert
o: Desert communities hold rich traditions about the desert
Deserts are one of the three main landforms in the chapter
Only people of cold deserts have folk songs and legends
Humans have never been able to adapt to living in deserts

questions.q: (a) A student says Antarctica cannot be a desert because it is icy and cold. Which part of the chapter's description of deserts lets some experts call it one? (b) Using (a), explain why a hot place with heavy rain every month would still not be a desert.
questions.a: (a) Deserts are described as large, dry expanses with very little precipitation; heat is not part of the description, and the chapter names a cold desert, the Gobi, so a cold, dry continent can count. (b) Heavy rain means a lot of precipitation, and a desert has very little; heat alone does not make a desert.
s: (a) Dryness and very little precipitation define a desert, not heat
(b) Heavy rain is plenty of precipitation, so heat alone is not enough

questions.q: Two ways of classifying land appear in the chapter: the three main landforms, and the five tinais of Tamil Sangam poetry. Which idea is built into the tinai scheme but NOT into the three-landform scheme?
questions.a: What people mainly do for work in each
o: What people mainly do for work in each
The height of the land above sea level
The shape of the land's top and its slopes
